articles.title: Every story has a shape

body.support:
Think of a film, a song or a post you watched to the end. Most of them have the same shape.

**1. Start.** We meet the **character**. Where are they? When?

**2. Problem.** Something goes wrong.

**3. Build-up.** It gets harder.

**4. Turning point.** The big moment. Everything changes.

**5. Ending.** How does it work out?

**It's everywhere.** You'll find this shape in:

- films
- songs
- ads
- posts and reels
- stories people tell at work.

**Who's it for? Why?** Every story is made for some people. That's the **audience**. It's made for a reason:

- to make you laugh
- to teach you something
- to sell you something
- to help you remember.
body.core:
Think about a film you loved, a song that tells a story, or a post you watched to the end. They look different. But most of them follow the same shape.

**1. Start.** We meet the **character** and the **setting**: who, where and when. Good stories often start with a **hook**: something that makes you want to keep watching.

**2. Problem.** Something goes wrong, or gets in the way of what the character wants. This is what keeps you hooked. No problem, no story.

**3. Build-up.** Things get harder. The character tries to fix it. The tension grows.

**4. Turning point.** The big moment when everything changes. A choice, a surprise, a phone call.

**5. Ending.** How it works out. Happy, sad, funny or a twist.

**It's everywhere.** You'll find this shape in:

- **films and short films**
- **songs** that tell a story
- **ads** (a problem, then the product saves the day)
- **social media posts** and reels
- **news features** about a real person
- the **yarns** people tell at work or at the pub.

**Who's it for, and why?** Every story is made for an **audience**, and for a **purpose**:

- to **entertain** (a comedy short)
- to **teach** (a safety video that tells a worker's story)
- to **sell** (an ad)
- to **remember** (a song about a real event).

The same shape gets used differently depending on who it's for. A story for kids is simple and safe. A story for adults can be complicated and dark. A 15-second ad has to do it all, fast.
body.extend:
Whether it's a feature film, a story-song, a 15-second ad or a reel, most narratives share an underlying structure.

**1. Orientation.** The audience meets the **character** and **setting**. Strong openings include a **hook** that creates curiosity.

**2. Complication.** A **problem** disrupts the character's world or blocks what they want. Conflict drives the story.

**3. Rising action.** Attempts to solve the problem raise the stakes and build tension.

**4. Climax.** The **turning point**: a decision, revelation or event that changes everything.

**5. Resolution.** The consequences play out, in an **ending** that may be happy, tragic, open or twisted.

**Across text types.** This structure appears in films and short films, narrative songs, advertisements (problem, then product as solution), social media content, feature journalism, and everyday anecdotes.

**Audience and purpose.** Creators shape the structure to suit their **audience** and **purpose**: to entertain, inform, persuade or commemorate. A children's story resolves neatly; adult fiction may leave questions open; an ad compresses the whole arc into seconds. Analysing those choices reveals what a text is trying to do, and to whom.

caseStudies.title: Tropfest: a whole story in 7 minutes

body.support:
**Tropfest** is a famous Australian short film festival. It started in **1993** in Sydney, at a café.

It has two big rules:

- Every film must be **seven minutes or less**.
- Every film must show the **Signature Item**. It's an object that changes each year. In 2026, it was an **hourglass**.

Seven minutes is short! So filmmakers hook you fast. They show the problem quickly. They get to the turning point. Then they end it.

You don't need a lot of time to tell a story. You need a clear shape.
body.core:
**Tropfest** is one of Australia's best-known short film festivals.

It was started in **1993** by actor and filmmaker **John Polson**. The first festival was called the Tropicana Short Film Festival, after a café in Sydney. It showed **nine** short films. It grew into a huge outdoor event, with crowds watching on big screens.

Tropfest has two big rules:

- Every film must be **seven minutes or less**, including the titles and credits.
- Every film must include the **Signature Item**: an object or idea that changes every year. It proves the film was made just for that festival. In 2026, the Signature Item was an **hourglass**.

Seven minutes is not much time. So filmmakers have to be clever. They hook you fast. They set up the problem quickly. They build to a turning point. And they land the ending before the timer runs out.

After some years off, Tropfest returned in **February 2026**, at Centennial Park in Sydney.

The lesson for your own stories: you don't need a lot of time. You need a clear shape.
body.extend:
**Tropfest** is among Australia's best-known short film festivals.

It was founded in **1993** by actor and filmmaker **John Polson**. The first event, named the Tropicana Short Film Festival after a Sydney café, showed **nine** films. It later grew into a major outdoor festival, screened to large crowds.

Two rules define it:

- Films must run **seven minutes or less**, including titles and credits.
- Every film must feature the year's **Signature Item**, which changes annually and shows the film was made for that festival. In 2026, the item was an **hourglass**.

The time limit forces tight structure. Filmmakers must establish character and setting, introduce a complication, build to a climax and resolve it, all within seven minutes. Every shot has to earn its place.

After several years away, Tropfest returned in **February 2026** at Centennial Park in Sydney.

For storytellers, the lesson is that length matters less than structure.

model.text:
**My story:** The day the dog ate my pay

**Start (who and where):** Me, last summer, after my first week of fruit picking. I had $200 cash in my pocket.

**Problem:** I left my shorts on the floor. Our dog, Biscuit, chews everything.

**Big moment:** I walked in. Biscuit looked up. A $50 note was hanging out of his mouth.

**End:** We taped three notes back together, and the bank swapped them. The fourth one? We never found it. Now I get paid into my account.

**How I will tell it:** Out loud to my group, with a pause before the big moment.

teacher.overview: Students learn the shape of a narrative (start, problem, build-up, turning point, ending), find it across films, songs, ads, reels and everyday yarns, and explain how stories are designed for audiences and purposes. They annotate a short film plan, sort story lines, map a story they know, plan with a storyboard, and tell a 60-second story. The case study is Tropfest, the Australian short film festival started in 1993, where films must be seven minutes or less and include a yearly Signature Item.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** start, problem, build-up, turning point, ending. E.g. films, songs, ads, posts, news features, yarns. E.g. entertain, teach, sell, remember.

**Film plan:** 1 hook; 2 start; 3 problem; 4 build-up; 5 turning point; 6 ending.

**Sort:** song — start; phone rang — turning point; car won't start — problem; Pickles — ending; coach — turning point; Jack — start.

**Case study:** the limit forces a tight, clear shape with nothing wasted; the Signature Item proves the film is new and made for the festival; audience: film fans, families and the general public at an outdoor event.

resources.label: AAP — Timely Tropfest return like sands through the hourglass

realityCheck: **Some students freeze on “a story”.** Let them tell a true story about something small: a bad shift, a funny moment, a lost phone.
**Filming is optional.** Telling it out loud counts.
**Keep content appropriate.** Remind students their audience is the class.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's quick, fun and builds confidence for later speaking courses.
